newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urged to reform forex intervention system.
newsitem.headline: Japan urged to reform forex intervention system.

text.p: Japanese monetary authorities are being urged to change the way they obtain financing to intervene in currency markets, and to follow other major G7 countries in making their operations more transparent.

"It is urgent that the monetary authorities undertake a full review of the entire mechanism for currency market intervention," said Sayuri Kawamura, a senior economist at Japan Research Institute Ltd.
Japan has the world's largest external reserves at $217.11 billion, with much of that accumulated over the past several years through aggressive dollar-buying intervention.

However, the Ministry of Finance (MOF), which decides when and at what amounts to intervene in the forex market, and the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the agent for the operations, have been reluctant to release any information on their actions.
The central banks of other Group of Seven (G7) countries, such as the U.S. Federal Reserve and Germany's Bundesbank, disclose information in their quarterly and annual reports.
Taisuke Tanaka, market strategist at Credit Suisse Tokyo, said that although more openness might limit the effectiveness of intervention, the public's right to know takes precedence.
"Preventing information from reaching the public may add to the effectiveness of intervention because the market impact can be maximised through secrecy and unexpectedness."
"But, given the general direction in which people demand that the government be more accountable in its financial operations, MOF, too, is obliged to give an explanation of its actions," Tanaka said.
Kawamura said a review should involve public discussion on whether intervention is cost-efficient and if such unlimited use of funds by the MOF for intervention is justifiable.
To foster debate, the monetary authorities must disclose more relevant data on intervention, including the actual sums used for intervention, she said.
MOF normally raises yen for intervention through the issue of special foreign exchange bills (FBs), which usually carry interest rates that are lower than prevailing market rates.

Due to the low yield, FBs are not always in great demand and the BOJ and other public entities are obligated to buy whatever issues are left unsold. Analysts say this financing method is at the core of the problem.
"It must be ideal for MOF to ensure a system that enables smooth access to funds at below market rates, particularly since forex policy has high priority in Japan," Tanaka said.

However, the large amount of cash made readily available to MOF for intervention has led to the large accumulation of external reserves, which in turn has exposed the government to significant foreign exchange risks, Tanaka added.
MOF data shows foreign exchange losses from past currency intervention are expected to top 10 trillion yen ($88.4 billion) by the end of this fiscal year in March 1997.
However, current accounting methods do not require MOF to realise these massive forex losses.
The issuing of FBs normally needs to be discussed and approved by parliament, but there is apparently no debate.
The financing mechanism for intervention has in reality led to the underwriting of government debt by the central bank, which is banned under Japanese law, Kawamura said.
FB purchases are also hurting the BOJ's portfolio as the central bank must unload holdings of other short-term securities with attractive yields to buy them.
The BOJ has made no secret of its discontent over MOF's reliance on the central bank to finance intervention.
Meanwhile, an influential academic group has proposed to a panel advising Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that the BOJ be banned from underwriting FBs. ($1=113 yen)
